=== FILE: videos/2017-03-14_bZ3i8djj2Yg_advanced-training-techniques/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: bZ3i8djj2Yg
title: "SSAC17: Advanced Training Techniques"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Brandon Payne, Blake (surname not stated; named as co-presenter and maker of the slides)]
topics: [basketball, sports-science, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Brandon Payne, who says he owns Accelerate Basketball, describes a ten-point training philosophy built over roughly eight or nine years and used with Stephen Curry. He says the philosophy came first and technology was added where it fit without slowing sessions. The argument is that a less explosive player can close the gap by training the brain along with the body, and that drills double as readiness assessments. Conditioning is redefined as keeping decision accuracy and speed when tired, tested by repeating a light-based decision drill after simulated quarters. The talk is a practitioner description with video clips. No data, sample sizes or outcomes are shown.

## Key claims

- Technology was added to a philosophy built in 2008 and 2009, not the other way round. [02:10]
- Curry would not top an NFL-style combine of explosive athletes, so the gap to more athletic players has to be closed another way. [05:44]
- Technology should not replace the player's own work, and overloading a player with it makes them shut it out. [08:20]
- The same philosophy is scaled from age three or four up to NBA players. Drill speed and implementation change, but the elements stay the same. [09:53]
- The tennis-ball and dribbling overload drill is an assessment, not a ball-handling drill. The coach watches for held breath, shoulders rocking (core not engaged) and knees buckling in. [10:55] [11:56]
- If any of those signs appear, the speaker concludes the brain-body link is not ready for accelerated learning that day. [12:26]
- Everyone has a physical ceiling. The aim is to reach it, then use the brain (decisions, efficiency) to operate past it. [13:27] [13:58]
- A headphone brain-stimulation product was added to physical activation in the past 18 months. The speaker says it looks good after reading the literature and cites no study. [14:28] [14:59]
- An oxygen mask is used to produce a winded state in stationary drills, not to build conditioning, so the offseason body is not stressed further. [16:31] [17:04]
- Light discs flash colours that map to assigned moves, and players sometimes freeze when several flash at once. The tool is used for decision-making and for grading conditioning. [18:06] [19:08]
- Every drill trains three movement elements: acceleration, deceleration and dynamic stability. Video is important for this. [19:40] [20:10]
- Conditioning tests that players must pass are not used. The aim is the same decision at the same speed at minute 48 as at minute one. [21:11] [21:42]
- Conditioning is graded by repeating a baseline decision drill after each simulated quarter. If fourth-quarter scores match pregame scores, the speaker says he knows the player is ready for 82 games. [23:15] [23:48]
- Overload and contrast (bands, heavy balls, accelerometers) is used to teach new movements. [24:19]
- Video and a shot-tracking product are used to see whether fatigue changes mechanics and shot arc, depth and location. [24:51] [25:21]
- Each drill is meant to serve several purposes, and a more body-aware player gets more from it. The drills also serve as feedback on readiness. [26:24] [26:57]
- Strength work is built from what opponents did to the player last season (physical defence), using medicine balls and trainers bumping the player, and avoids fixed patterns. [27:29] [27:59]

## Numbers and definitions

- Curry at 165 pounds at Davidson. [00:36] (caption splits the sentence across [00:36] and [01:07])
- Two-time MVP, one unanimous. [01:07] [07:16]
- Company started 2008 and 2009; philosophy worked on "eight or nine years"; ten points. [00:36] [02:10] [02:42]
- Scales from three- and four-year-olds to NBA. [09:53]
- Product used for the past 18 months. [14:28]
- Four light discs, one to three flash at a time. [18:06]
- Decision-point distances: about 14 feet, then 10 feet, then six feet. [22:13] [22:45] (the 14 is split across the two blocks; treat as lightly uncertain)
- One simulated quarter takes about five minutes, with no fouls or dead balls. [22:45]
- Four quarters tested and compared with the pregame score; 82 games. [23:15]
- Workouts can be 30, 90 or 120 minutes, and a nominal 90 can shrink to 30. [13:58] [14:28]
- 48 minutes as the comparison point. [21:42]
- Defined: "conditioning" here means decision accuracy and speed held under fatigue. [21:42]

## Methods and frameworks named

- A ten-point philosophy; only some points are covered (physical activation, neuromuscular activation, cognitive development, three movement elements, performance capacity, overload and contrast, high-volume reps at game speed, multiple tasks, on-court strength, systematic muscle confusion).
- Conditioning assessment: baseline light-based decision drill with closing distance, then four simulated quarters, with the drill repeated after each and compared on time and score.
- Drill-as-assessment checklist: breathing, shoulder movement, knee position.
- Tools named in captions: iPad brain games, light discs (caption spelling "fitlike"), headphone stimulation product (caption "neuro Halo"), oxygen mask, "vertox" (caption spelling), shot analyzer (caption "Noah"), video.

## Limits and open questions

- One elite athlete, anecdotes and clips. No reliability, validity or outcome data.
- Product claims (headphones, shot analyzer) are the speaker's view; he cites no study.
- The speaker owns a training business and is describing his own method.
- "Ready for 82 games" is a judgement from a drill comparison, not a validated threshold.
- The fatigue block is not shown to be standard across athletes or sessions.
- Caption problems: introducer name is garbled ("Michael Gan Angeli"); several product names are misspelled; the sentence about Curry's college weight is garbled around [01:07].

## Q&A

No Q&A. The speaker says time is short and ends the talk. [29:02]

type: video-summary
video_id: oFXTlvyFma8
title: "SSAC17: Player Grades: The Competitive Advantage in Football Performance"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Chris Collinssworth (caption spelling), Neil Hornsby; introduced by Barry Brney (caption spelling)]
topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Chris Collinssworth (caption spelling) and Neil Hornsby, founder of Pro Football Focus, present how PFF grades football players. Collinssworth argues that analysts are taking over decisions once left to veteran coaches. Hornsby explains that grades come from analysts watching every play, and that raw grades are then adjusted for the quality of each opportunity, such as time to throw, step drop, down and distance and alignment. He says grades score what should have happened on a play, not its result, and are a production measure that ignores injury and talent. A coach is shown saying he disagreed with about a dozen of about 600 plays. A Q&A follows.

## Key claims

- PFF was working with 25 teams, expecting 28 or 30, and the speakers say data analysts now make decisions once left to coaches. [01:16] [01:46]
- Raw grades are a blunt instrument. They must be turned into player grades by adjusting for the opportunity behind them. [13:05]
- Counting opportunities is not enough. A tackle with 450 pass blocks can have faced more total time than one with 550, because the quarterback holds the ball longer. [14:07] [14:39]
- Factors named: time to throw, step drop, help or chips, slide protection, down and distance, opponent technique. [15:09] [15:40]
- Each player has a raw grade plus a normalization factor that compares the player with average. [16:11]
- Screens and rollouts are removed from the pass-rush set because they limit the chance to get pressure. [16:43] [17:14]
- Alignment matters: chance of pressure rises as a rusher lines up further from the centre. [17:14]
- Step drop matters: a rusher against a quarterback who takes many seven-step drops has more chance than one against a quarterback taking many three-step drops. [18:16] [18:46]
- Down and distance matters: a situational third-down rusher has more chance than a rusher who must also play the run. [19:16]
- Fatigue (number of rush attempts) showed noise over ten years, so it is left out. [19:49]
- A new process planned for 2017 will record matchup, block type, block location, how well it was done and the pass-rush move, to test whether assignment difficulty matters. The speaker does not know the answer. [21:51] [22:22] [22:53]
- An offensive line coach says he disagreed with about a dozen of about 600 negative plays and that the grades are close to what the players are. [24:25] [25:28]
- Grades are by position. Ranking across positions needs separate maths. [27:30] [28:02]
- Grading is done by about 350 people on a cloud system, with a second pass, a coach-network pass, then adjustment. [29:44] [30:15]
- Grades score what should have happened, not the result. The example is a game with five touchdown passes and no interceptions graded near zero. [31:17] [31:47] [32:17]
- Opponent-quality adjustment is done after grades are published, by looking at who a player faced. Matchup data will allow it directly. [32:56] [33:27] [33:58]
- PFF Ultimate is a tool to ask football questions and send answers to video or charts. [26:28]
- The data go back ten years, and old seasons are graded too (2006 last year). [16:43] [38:37] [39:08]
- The grade is a production metric for how a player is playing now. It ignores injury, talent and, at the moment, who was faced. [39:40]
- One speaker is less enamoured with red-zone statistics and says the game between the 20s differs from the game inside the 20. [37:05] [37:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- 25 teams now; 28 or 30 expected; about 20 teams met. [01:16]
- 300 to 350 people; 350 analysts. [02:16] [08:54]
- 30 quarterback disruptions in 450 or 550 pass blocks. [13:37]
- Seven-step drop, quarterback at 10 yards, rusher taken to 11 yards. [18:16]
- About 600 plays (two thirds of the season; caption garbled), disagreement with about a dozen. [24:25]
- Grade of 84 said to mean nothing to viewers; ranking instead, for example "number 117 of 117". [27:30]
- About 15 years average NFL coaching in the coach network; about 20 people can input at once. [29:44] [30:15]
- Ten years of data. [16:43]
- Definition: production metric = how the player is playing now, excluding injury, talent and opponent strength. [39:40]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Analysts grade every play, with multiple passes and coach review, producing raw grades.
- Opportunity normalization: adjust raw grade for time to throw, step drop, down and distance, alignment, help, and exclusions (screens, rollouts).
- Point-of-attack tapes built from raw grades for each player. [12:34]
- Grade by what should have happened on the play, not the outcome.
- 2017 matchup and block-type data project to test assignment difficulty.

## Limits and open questions

- Accuracy evidence shown is one coach's disagreement count (about a dozen of about 600), reported as small.
- Neither speaker gives the grade scale or the weights in the normalization.
- Collinssworth says he bought the company [08:54], and Hornsby sells the grades, so claims about accuracy are the vendors' view.
- Opponent strength is not yet in the grade, which the speaker admits. [39:40]
- Whether assignment difficulty matters is stated as unknown. [22:53]
- The captions garble parts of the Q&A, notably [30:45]. A talk about wide-receiver or evaluation (question) cannot be recovered.
- Mostly NFL examples; the FBS level is mentioned but no college results are shown.

## Q&A

- How is grading done by hand, and can it be automated? Answer: cloud input, multiple passes, coach network, then maths. [29:44]
- Question from a wide receiver (garbled caption). The answer says PFF grades should-have-happened, unlike league statistics. [30:45] [31:17]
- Why not adjust for above-average opposition in the grade? Answer: done after publication; matchup data will do it. [32:56]
- Value of the data set and uses beyond football (partly garbled). Answer: ten years of depth, possibly other sports. [34:29] [36:03]
- Red-zone statistics. Answer: personal scepticism; and a view that the game differs inside the 20. [36:34] [37:05]
- Grading history (Hall of Fame debates) and training new analysts. [38:37]

title: "SSAC17: Marijuana As Medicine"
event: SSAC17 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

topics: [american-football, injury-health, policy]

## Summary

Andrew Brant (caption spelling), a former agent who says he worked for the Green Bay Packers for ten years, argues that growing public acceptance of marijuana is unlikely to reach the NFL through recreational use but may through pain management. He explains that NFL rules come from the collective bargaining agreement, not state law, outlines the league's staged testing and penalties, and notes a raised positive threshold. He links the issue to opioid and Toradol use, to advocacy by former players, and to concern about concussions. His view is that change will need to come through bargaining or be framed as health and safety. It is a policy talk, not a study.

## Key claims

- The talk asks whether societal acceptance will carry over into sports leagues, mainly as a pain-management tool, with the NFL as the focus. [00:31] [01:01]
- State legalization does not let NFL players use marijuana, because they are governed by the collective bargaining agreement. [06:14] [06:45]
- Marijuana policy is negotiated and not discretionary, unlike the personal conduct policy. [07:49] [08:21]
- A revised drug policy added HGH testing and, in exchange, raised the marijuana positive threshold. [08:51]
- The speaker's view is that traction will come on medicinal use and pain management, not recreational use. [16:11]
- A newspaper study is cited saying one in four players felt pressure from team doctors to take opioids. [16:44]
- From his own experience, Toradol was overprescribed and overused in the NFL. [17:46] [18:20]
- Advocacy has to come from players, and former players fill the gap because active players risk stigma and have little contract protection. [18:51] [22:32]
- Eugene Monroe is described as a former lineman who says he was handed opioids early, had problems from overuse, and found marijuana better for pain. [19:53] [20:26]
- Concussion concern may be the route to getting owners to listen, and Monroe has donated to Johns Hopkins and Pennsylvania for study. [20:58] [21:30]
- The NFL has followed the science on concussions, and the speaker expects kickoff returns to disappear within five years. [23:34]
- The NFL tends to follow other leagues and avoid being a first mover on taboo subjects. [24:05]
- Change would need a bargaining trade, or a framing as health and safety, which he calls a tough sell. [26:41] [27:43]
- He does not expect another revision before the agreement ends in 2021. [26:41]

## Numbers and definitions

- 2016 ballot measures; 21 states allowing medicinal use, nine allowing recreational use including DC, and 21 illegal (caption ambiguous). [05:12]
- Positive threshold raised from 15 to 35 nanograms per millilitre; MLB at 15; the world anti-doping body at 115 (caption names are garbled: "anagrams", "water world anti-doping Association"). [09:23]
- Testing window April 20th to August 9th. [10:55] [11:26]
- Stage 1: 90-day treatment plan; violation fine of three of 17 weeks' pay (caption reads "317"). [12:28] [12:59]
- Stage 2: up to 10 tests a month, four hours to give a sample, 12 to 24 months; first violation a two-week fine versus four weeks for performance-enhancing drugs; second violation leads to a four-to-six-game suspension. [12:59] [13:30] [14:01] [14:35]
- Stage 3: ten-game suspension, then one-year banishment with reapplication; the stage 2 testing regime continues for the rest of the career. [15:06] [15:38] (caption says "in Italy", likely garbled)
- Opioid study: 25 percent felt pressure; "7%" taking them at three times the national rate (caption ambiguous). [16:44]
- Collective bargaining agreement ends 2021. [26:41]
- Fourteen padded practices in season. [28:14]
- About 95 percent of brains tested for CTE at BU (caption says "95%"), a sample he calls slanted. [31:09] [31:39]

## Methods and frameworks named

- The staged NFL testing and penalty system.
- A bargaining frame: marijuana as a trade item versus a health-and-safety issue like concussions.
- The "follow the science" frame borrowed from concussion policy.

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker repeatedly says he is not a scientist [09:23] [28:14]; claims on cannabis for pain and CTE cite no study, and the Washington Post study is not shown.
- He is a former agent and team executive, so his bargaining views are his own.
- Anecdotes: Packers Toradol, Eugene Monroe's account, and players he says he knows.
- Predictions (kickoff returns gone, no policy change before 2021) are opinions.
- NFL only; the talk does not cover college or other leagues' details.
- Monroe's quotes are advocacy and the talk does not test them.
- Captions garble league names and units at [09:23] and [15:06].

## Q&A

- How much capacity does the NFL have to act given state-by-state law? Answer: through bargaining; medicinal use is possible with scientific and doctor involvement, with owner resistance. [29:34] [30:06]
- CTE and the concussion settlement. Answer: the settlement covers dementia, Alzheimer's, ALS and Parkinson's, not CTE; CTE sampling is skewed toward players with symptoms; he says studies show cannabis helps pain management for CTE, without naming one. [30:38] [31:39] [32:09]

Caption problems and unverifiable claims: auto captions garble names (Michael Gan Angeli, Rob mirandy, Barry Brney, "anagrams"/"water world anti-doping", "317", "Italy") and the wide-receiver Q&A at [30:45] in video 2; unverifiable: the Washington Post opioid statistic and the cannabis/CTE claim (video 3), the "ready for 82 games" and headphone claims (video 1), and PFF accuracy (video 2); no Q&A in video 1; the "[08:54] bought the company" attribution to Collinssworth in video 2 rests on a caption that says "I bought the company".
